messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 30
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bank Teller
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 56

# Maria's Story

Maria sits in the waiting room each week with her hands folded tightly in her lap, her wedding ring catching the fluorescent light. At thirty, she carries herself with the careful precision of someone who has learned to take up as little space as possible. She works as a bank teller at a downtown branch, a job she's held for seven years—a position that now feels both necessary and impossible.

Five years ago, Maria was traveling through Central America on what was supposed to be a transformative gap year. She'd saved for two years, dreaming of volunteer work and self-discovery. Instead, she was in the wrong place during a political uprising. She was taken from her hostel by armed men she still cannot fully describe without her voice becoming hollow. For three weeks, she was held in a concrete room with six other people. The details come out slowly, in fragments—the sound of the door, the specific way her captors smelled, the cold of the floor at night. She was interrogated repeatedly, though she had nothing to tell them. They didn't seem to care. The interrogations were about something else entirely.

When she was finally released in a prisoner exchange, she weighed twenty pounds less than when she'd been taken. Her family flew to meet her in a hospital in Mexico City. She returned home physically, though something essential remained behind in that room.

The first year back, Maria couldn't leave her house. She lost her job at the bank, then regained it when her therapist at the time insisted she needed structure. She's been returning to work for four years now, but it remains a daily negotiation with her own nervous system. The bank's security door makes a specific buzzing sound when it locks behind her. Every time she hears it, her body floods with adrenaline. She knows logically that she's safe, that this is a normal bank door in a normal city, but her body doesn't believe her. Her heart races. Her hands shake as she counts out bills. Sometimes she has to excuse herself to the bathroom and sit in a stall for ten minutes, breathing deliberately until her hands stop trembling.

She's married now to James, whom she met two years after returning home. He's patient in the way only someone truly committed can be. But Maria struggles with intimacy. She freezes sometimes when he touches her unexpectedly, even when she knows he's coming. She has nightmares most nights—not always about the captivity itself, but about being trapped, unable to move, unable to call for help. She wakes gasping, sometimes striking out before she's fully conscious. James absorbs this without complaint, but she sees the exhaustion in his face.

What troubles Maria most is how unpredictable her reactions have become. Last month, a regular customer came through her line speaking a language that sounded like the one her captors used. She didn't finish her shift. She called James from the break room, unable to articulate what was wrong, and he had to come pick her up. She sat in the car with her eyes fixed on nothing, her body rigid, unable to explain.

She describes feeling like she's living in two timelines simultaneously. In one, she's a competent woman doing her job, managing a marriage, moving through days. In the other, she's still in that room, still waiting for the door to open, still unsure if she'll survive. The two timelines overlap constantly, and she never knows which one will be real in any given moment.
